power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: When Unusual Is Usual: Multivariate Analysis of WAIS-5 Index Score Profiles

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychological Medicine
								University of Otago
								
									Wellington
									New Zealand

text.text: Interpretation of cognitive profiles commonly involves the identification of low scores, discrepancies and relative strengths and weaknesses.
However, a finding that is unusual when considered individually may be considerably less unusual within a person's broader cognitive profile.
To account for this, Crawford et al. (2012) developed a multivariate approach that placed individual WAIS-IV findings within their wider normative context.
text.formatted: To account for this, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref> developed a multivariate approach that placed individual WAIS-IV findings within their wider normative context.

text.text: The present study extends this approach to the five primary indices of the WAIS-5.

Monte Carlo simulation of 1,000,000 normative profiles was used to estimate base rates for four complementary aspects of profile interpretation: the rarity of the overall index-score configuration using the Mahalanobis Distance Index (MDI), multiple low index scores, multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies, and multiple relative strengths and weaknesses.

Individually unusual findings occurred substantially more frequently when considered across the complete profile, particularly for pairwise discrepancies, where ten overlapping comparisons are possible.
The MDI provided complementary information about the rarity of the complete five-index configuration and was more strongly associated with within-profile variability than with overall score level.

Together with the accompanying clinical calculator, these analyses provide an accessible framework for placing individual findings and broader patterns of WAIS-5 performance within their normative context.
Distinguishing potentially unusual cognitive test scores from the variation commonly seen in healthy individuals represents a significant challenge in neuropsychological assessment.

Research in healthy populations has shown substantial within-person variability in neuropsychological performance, including the occurrence of low scores and marked differences between cognitive abilities (Schretlen et al., 2003; Binder et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Research in healthy populations has shown substantial within-person variability in neuropsychological performance, including the occurrence of low scores and marked differences between cognitive abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Schretlen et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Binder et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, a finding that appears unusual when considered individually may not be unusual when viewed within the person's broader profile, particularly as the number of scores examined increases (Binder et al., 2009; Kiselica et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Consequently, a finding that appears unusual when considered individually may not be unusual when viewed within the person's broader profile, particularly as the number of scores examined increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Binder et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kiselica et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is therefore important to consider not only how unusual an individual finding is but how unusual it is to observe that finding, or several such findings, within the person's profile as a whole.
One way of addressing this problem is through the use of multivariate base-rate methods.

These methods estimate how frequently unusual findings occur when multiple cognitive measures are considered together, allowing an individual finding to be interpreted within the context of the wider assessment (Crawford et al., 2007; Kiselica et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These methods estimate how frequently unusual findings occur when multiple cognitive measures are considered together, allowing an individual finding to be interpreted within the context of the wider assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kiselica et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Their use has become increasingly established in neuropsychological interpretation, with Kiselica et al. (2024) identifying 67 papers involving multivariate base-rate methods in a recent review.
text.formatted: Their use has become increasingly established in neuropsychological interpretation, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kiselica et al. (2024)</ref> identifying 67 papers involving multivariate base-rate methods in a recent review.

text.text: By taking account of the relationships among cognitive measures, these methods can also estimate how unusual a particular pattern of performance is within the normative population (Crawford et al., 2007; Huizenga et al., 2016).
text.formatted: By taking account of the relationships among cognitive measures, these methods can also estimate how unusual a particular pattern of performance is within the normative population <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Huizenga et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A particularly comprehensive application of multivariate methods to cognitive profile interpretation has been developed by Crawford and colleagues. Crawford et al. (2012) applied these methods to the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Fourth Edition (WAIS-IV; Wechsler, 2008), asking how unusual different features of an individual's profile were within the normative population.
text.formatted: A particularly comprehensive application of multivariate methods to cognitive profile interpretation has been developed by <ref type="bibr">Crawford and colleagues. Crawford et al. (2012)</ref> applied these methods to the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Fourth Edition (WAIS-IV; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Wechsler, 2008)</ref>, asking how unusual different features of an individual's profile were within the normative population.

text.text: Building on earlier work (Crawford et al., 2007; Crawford & Allan, 1994), they examined the overall configuration of index scores, the occurrence of multiple low scores and unusual pairwise discrepancies, and strengths and weaknesses relative to an individual's own mean level of performance.
text.formatted: Building on earlier work <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Crawford & Allan, 1994)</ref>, they examined the overall configuration of index scores, the occurrence of multiple low scores and unusual pairwise discrepancies, and strengths and weaknesses relative to an individual's own mean level of performance.

text.text: Together, these methods provided a broad framework for evaluating the normative rarity of different features of WAIS-IV performance.
The release of the WAIS-5 creates an opportunity to revisit these multivariate methods.

The WAIS-5 provides five primary index scores and normative procedures for evaluating individual pairwise discrepancies and relative strengths and weaknesses (Wechsler et al., 2025a (Wechsler et al., , 2025b)).
text.formatted: The WAIS-5 provides five primary index scores and normative procedures for evaluating individual pairwise discrepancies and relative strengths and weaknesses <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Wechsler et al., 2025a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Wechsler et al., , 2025b))</ref>.

text.text: However, it does not provide corresponding base rates for the occurrence of multiple low index scores, multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies, or multiple relative strengths and weaknesses within the same profile, nor an estimate of the rarity of the complete five-index configuration.
This is particularly relevant because five primary indices generate ten possible pairwise comparisons, compared with six among the four primary WAIS-IV indices examined by Crawford et al. (2012).
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant because five primary indices generate ten possible pairwise comparisons, compared with six among the four primary WAIS-IV indices examined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>.

text.text: These comparisons are not independent: each index contributes to four pairwise differences, meaning that several unusual discrepancies can arise from the same feature of a profile.
The frequency of such patterns therefore needs to be considered within the relationships among the complete set of index scores (Crawford et al., 2007 (Crawford et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: The frequency of such patterns therefore needs to be considered within the relationships among the complete set of index scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: The present study therefore sought to replicate and extend the framework developed by Crawford et al. (2012) for the five primary index scores of the WAIS-5.
text.formatted: The present study therefore sought to replicate and extend the framework developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref> for the five primary index scores of the WAIS-5.

text.text: Four complementary aspects of profile interpretation were examined: the rarity of the overall five-index profile, the occurrence of multiple low index scores, multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies, and multiple relative strengths and weaknesses around an individual's Mean Index Score.

Monte Carlo simulation was used to estimate the normative frequency of these profile characteristics while accounting for the relationships among the five indices, consistent with established multivariate base-rate methods (Crawford et al., 2007 (Crawford et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: Monte Carlo simulation was used to estimate the normative frequency of these profile characteristics while accounting for the relationships among the five indices, consistent with established multivariate base-rate methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: In keeping with Crawford et al. (2012), a clinical calculator was also developed to make these analyses readily accessible for use alongside routine WAIS-5 interpretation.
text.formatted: In keeping with <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>, a clinical calculator was also developed to make these analyses readily accessible for use alongside routine WAIS-5 interpretation.

text.text: The present study involved secondary analysis of published aggregate psychometric data and statistical modelling only.
No participant-level or identifiable data were collected or accessed.
The study therefore did not require formal institutional ethics approval.

To examine the normative rarity of WAIS-5 cognitive profiles, four complementary analyses were undertaken following the approach developed by Crawford and colleagues (Crawford et al., 2007 (Crawford et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: To examine the normative rarity of WAIS-5 cognitive profiles, four complementary analyses were undertaken following the approach developed by Crawford and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: The configuration of the five primary index scores was first evaluated using the Mahalanobis Distance Index (MDI; Mahalanobis, 1936), extending Crawford et al.'s four-index WAIS-IV approach to the five-index WAIS-5.
text.formatted: The configuration of the five primary index scores was first evaluated using the Mahalanobis Distance Index (MDI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Mahalanobis, 1936)</ref>, extending Crawford et al.'s four-index WAIS-IV approach to the five-index WAIS-5.

text.text: Three further analyses examined specific characteristics of the profile: the frequency of multiple low primary index scores, multiple unusual pairwise index discrepancies, and multiple relative strengths and weaknesses compared with the individual's Mean Index Score (MIS).

Analyses were based on the published intercorrelations among the five primary WAIS-5 indices: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), and Processing Speed (PSI), obtained from the Australian & New Zealand WAIS-5 Technical and Interpretive Manual (Wechsler et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: Analyses were based on the published intercorrelations among the five primary WAIS-5 indices: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), and Processing Speed (PSI), obtained from the Australian & New Zealand WAIS-5 Technical and Interpretive Manual <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Wechsler et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: Following the method of Crawford et al. (2012), the published intercorrelations were converted to a covariance matrix and used to define the multivariate normative model for subsequent analyses.
text.formatted: Following the method of <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>, the published intercorrelations were converted to a covariance matrix and used to define the multivariate normative model for subsequent analyses.

text.text: Following Crawford et al. (2007 Crawford et al. ( , 2012)), Monte Carlo simulation was used to estimate normative base rates for characteristics of WAIS-5 cognitive profiles.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Crawford et al. (2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. ( , 2012))</ref>, Monte Carlo simulation was used to estimate normative base rates for characteristics of WAIS-5 cognitive profiles.

text.text: Monte Carlo methods involve generating large numbers of synthetic observations from specified statistical parameters to model the expected behaviour of a distribution (Robert & Casella, 2004).
text.formatted: Monte Carlo methods involve generating large numbers of synthetic observations from specified statistical parameters to model the expected behaviour of a distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Robert & Casella, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Crawford and colleagues have previously used this approach to estimate the frequency of multiple low scores and other profile abnormalities across neuropsychological measures (Crawford et al., 2007 (Crawford et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: Crawford and colleagues have previously used this approach to estimate the frequency of multiple low scores and other profile abnormalities across neuropsychological measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: Monte Carlo simulations and statistical analyses were conducted in Python using NumPy, pandas, and SciPy packages.
Using the published WAIS-5 parameters, 1,000,000 cognitive profiles were generated from a five-dimensional multivariate normal distribution.
Each simulated profile comprised five correlated primary index scores and represented a hypothetical observation from the normative population.
This simulated population was then used to estimate normative base rates for the profile characteristics described below.

As checks on the computational implementation of the multivariate model, the means, standard deviations, and intercorrelations of the simulated index scores were compared with the specified WAIS-5 parameters (Wechsler et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: As checks on the computational implementation of the multivariate model, the means, standard deviations, and intercorrelations of the simulated index scores were compared with the specified WAIS-5 parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Wechsler et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: Analytical SD Dev and SD Diff values were also compared with their Monte Carlo equivalents.

Finally, because squared Mahalanobis distances are evaluated against a χ² distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of variables (Crawford et al., 2012), the simulated MDI distribution and tail probabilities were compared with their theoretical values under the χ² distribution with five degrees of freedom.
text.formatted: Finally, because squared Mahalanobis distances are evaluated against a χ² distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., 2012)</ref>, the simulated MDI distribution and tail probabilities were compared with their theoretical values under the χ² distribution with five degrees of freedom.

text.text: The Mahalanobis Distance Index (MDI), proposed for the analysis of cognitive profiles by Huba (1985) and subsequently applied to the Wechsler scales by Burgess (1991) and Crawford and Allan (1994), provides a measure of how unusual a configuration of scores is within a multivariate normative distribution.
text.formatted: The Mahalanobis Distance Index (MDI), proposed for the analysis of cognitive profiles by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Huba (1985)</ref> and subsequently applied to the Wechsler scales by <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Burgess (1991)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Crawford and Allan (1994)</ref>, provides a measure of how unusual a configuration of scores is within a multivariate normative distribution.

text.text: Mahalanobis distance quantifies how far an observation lies from the centre of a multivariate distribution while accounting for the covariance among variables (Mahalanobis, 1936).
text.formatted: Mahalanobis distance quantifies how far an observation lies from the centre of a multivariate distribution while accounting for the covariance among variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Mahalanobis, 1936)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly relevant to cognitive profiles because index scores are correlated, meaning that the rarity of a particular combination of scores cannot be determined by considering each score independently. Crawford et al. (2012) subsequently extended this approach to the four WAIS-IV index scores, providing a measure of the statistical rarity of the overall configuration of index scores.

(2012)</ref> subsequently extended this approach to the four WAIS-IV index scores, providing a measure of the statistical rarity of the overall configuration of index scores.

text.text: Following Crawford et al. (2012), the MDI was calculated for each WAIS-5 profile using the five index scores, normative mean vector, and covariance matrix.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>, the MDI was calculated for each WAIS-5 profile using the five index scores, normative mean vector, and covariance matrix.

text.text: Under multivariate normality, squared Mahalanobis distances follow a chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of variables.
The rarity associated with each MDI value was therefore estimated from the χ² distribution with five degrees of freedom (Crawford & Allan, 1994).
text.formatted: The rarity associated with each MDI value was therefore estimated from the χ² distribution with five degrees of freedom <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Crawford & Allan, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: As a validation check, the simulated MDI distribution was compared with the theoretical χ²(5) distribution, including selected percentile values and tail probabilities.
To assist interpretation of the MDI, its association with two readily interpretable characteristics of the cognitive profile was also examined across the simulated normative sample.

Overall level was represented by the absolute difference between the mean of the five index scores and the normative mean of 100, while within-profile variability was represented by the standard deviation of the five index scores.
Spearman correlations were calculated between the MDI and each of these profile characteristics.
Low scores occur with appreciable frequency in healthy individuals and become increasingly likely as more cognitive scores are examined (Binder et al., 2009; Crawford et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Low scores occur with appreciable frequency in healthy individuals and become increasingly likely as more cognitive scores are examined <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Binder et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Crawford et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Interpretation of low scores therefore requires consideration of both their number within a cognitive profile and the frequency with which such patterns occur in the normative population (Binder et al., 2009; Crawford et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Interpretation of low scores therefore requires consideration of both their number within a cognitive profile and the frequency with which such patterns occur in the normative population <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Binder et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Crawford et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Following Crawford et al. (2012), each simulated WAIS-5 profile was classified according to the number of primary index scores falling below the 25th, 15th, 10th, 5th, 2nd and 1st percentiles.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>, each simulated WAIS-5 profile was classified according to the number of primary index scores falling below the 25th, 15th, 10th, 5th, 2nd and 1st percentiles.

text.text: The percentage of simulated profiles containing at least one, two, three, four, or five low index scores was then calculated for each criterion.
The WAIS-5 manual provides empirical base rates for individual pairwise index discrepancies, reported separately according to which index is higher.

The present analysis addressed the complementary profile-level question examined by Crawford et al. (2012): how frequently multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies occur within a single cognitive profile.
text.formatted: The present analysis addressed the complementary profile-level question examined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>: how frequently multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies occur within a single cognitive profile.

text.text: This distinction is important because the probability of observing one or more unusual discrepancies increases when multiple comparisons are examined, meaning that the rarity of an individual discrepancy does not indicate the rarity of observing multiple unusual discrepancies within the profile as a whole (Crawford et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This distinction is important because the probability of observing one or more unusual discrepancies increases when multiple comparisons are examined, meaning that the rarity of an individual discrepancy does not indicate the rarity of observing multiple unusual discrepancies within the profile as a whole <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Differences were calculated for all 10 possible pairs of the five primary index scores.

The expected standard deviation of each pairwise difference (SD Diff ) was derived from the WAIS-5 covariance matrix and used to express each discrepancy relative to its normative distribution. Crawford et al. (2012) used two-tailed probabilities when evaluating pairwise discrepancies.
text.formatted: The expected standard deviation of each pairwise difference (SD Diff ) was derived from the WAIS-5 covariance matrix and used to express each discrepancy relative to its normative distribution. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref> used two-tailed probabilities when evaluating pairwise discrepancies.

text.text: The present analyses instead used directional probabilities to correspond with the WAIS-5 manual, which reports empirical base rates separately, according to which index is higher.
Each discrepancy was therefore evaluated according to how often a difference of that size or larger occurs in the same direction.
Discrepancies meeting the same rarity criterion were then counted together, regardless of direction.
Monte Carlo simulation was used to estimate the percentage of normative profiles containing increasing numbers of unusual pairwise discrepancies at rarity criteria ranging from 25% to 1%.
As a validation check, the resulting directional discrepancy thresholds were compared with the corresponding empirical thresholds reported in the WAIS-5 manual.

The WAIS-5 normative supplement (Wechsler et al., 2025b) provides procedures for identifying relative strengths and weaknesses by comparing each primary index score with the individual's own average (MIS).
text.formatted: The WAIS-5 normative supplement <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Wechsler et al., 2025b)</ref> provides procedures for identifying relative strengths and weaknesses by comparing each primary index score with the individual's own average (MIS).

text.text: In addition to determining whether a difference is statistically significant, the manual provides empirical base rates indicating how frequently strengths and weaknesses of a given magnitude occur in the normative sample.
These base rates are reported separately for strengths and weaknesses.
The present analysis extends this approach from individual strengths and weaknesses to the profile as a whole.
Specifically, we estimated how frequently normative profiles contain multiple strengths and weaknesses meeting a given rarity criterion.
For each simulated profile, the MIS was calculated as the arithmetic mean of the five primary index scores, and each index was expressed as a deviation from the MIS.

Following Crawford et al. (2012), the expected standard deviation of these deviations (SD Dev ) was calculated separately for each index from the WAIS-5 covariance structure and used to standardise the deviations.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>, the expected standard deviation of these deviations (SD Dev ) was calculated separately for each index from the WAIS-5 covariance structure and used to standardise the deviations.

text.text: As with pairwise differences, Crawford et al. (2012) used two-tailed probabilities when estimating the frequency of multiple unusual deviations.
text.formatted: As with pairwise differences, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref> used two-tailed probabilities when estimating the frequency of multiple unusual deviations.

text.text: We again modified this procedure to correspond more closely with the WAIS-5 strength/weakness analysis, in which base rates are reported separately for strengths and weaknesses.
Each simulated strength or weakness was therefore evaluated using a one-tailed probability.
Strengths and weaknesses meeting the same rarity criterion were then counted together within each profile.

Monte Carlo simulation was used to estimate the percentage of normative profiles containing at least one, two, three, four, or five strengths or weaknesses at the 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, and 1% rarity criteria.
With the exception of the MDI, the multivariate base rates described above can be tabulated in advance and applied clinically using lookup tables.
The MDI, in contrast, requires calculation for the individual's specific combination of index scores and involves matrix operations, making routine manual calculation impractical.

Consistent with Crawford et al. (2012), who provided accompanying software to implement their WAIS-IV procedures, a calculator was developed to facilitate clinical application of the present analyses.
text.formatted: Consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>, who provided accompanying software to implement their WAIS-IV procedures, a calculator was developed to facilitate clinical application of the present analyses.

text.text: The calculator accepts the five primary index scores and provides results for the MDI, multiple low scores, pairwise discrepancies, and relative strengths and weaknesses.
An optional FSIQ can also be entered to provide contextual information about the individual's overall level of performance; FSIQ does not contribute to any of the multivariate calculations.

The Monte Carlo simulation closely reproduced the published WAIS-5 psychometric parameters.

The simulated means and standard deviations closely reproduced their specified normative values (Supplementary Table S1), and the maximum absolute difference between simulated and published intercorrelations was .0013 (Supplementary Table S2).
text.formatted: The simulated means and standard deviations closely reproduced their specified normative values (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>), and the maximum absolute difference between simulated and published intercorrelations was .0013 (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Analytical SD Dev and SD Diff values were also closely reproduced by their Monte Carlo equivalents (Supplementary Table S3).
text.formatted: Analytical SD Dev and SD Diff values were also closely reproduced by their Monte Carlo equivalents (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Finally, the simulated MDI distribution closely approximated the theoretical χ² distribution with five degrees of freedom: the simulated mean and variance were 5.001 and 9.982, respectively, compared with theoretical values of 5.000 and 10.000, and simulated tail probabilities differed from their theoretical expectations by no more than 0.032 percentage points (Supplementary Tables S4 and S5).
text.formatted: Finally, the simulated MDI distribution closely approximated the theoretical χ² distribution with five degrees of freedom: the simulated mean and variance were 5.001 and 9.982, respectively, compared with theoretical values of 5.000 and 10.000, and simulated tail probabilities differed from their theoretical expectations by no more than 0.032 percentage points (Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S4</ref> and <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: Collectively, these checks indicated that the analytical procedures and Monte Carlo simulation accurately reproduced the specified WAIS-5 multivariate normative model.
The MDI evaluates how unusual the configuration of an individual's five primary index scores is, taking account of the correlations among the indices.
Larger MDI values indicate configurations that are increasingly unusual within the normative multivariate distribution.
The distribution of MDI values closely approximated the theoretical χ² distribution with five degrees of freedom.
The simulated mean was 5.001 compared with the theoretical value of 5.000, and the simulated variance was 9.982 compared with the theoretical value of 10.000.
Similarly, the simulated 95th and 99th percentiles were 11.070 and 15.072, respectively, compared with theoretical values of 11.071 and 15.086 (Supplementary Table S4).
text.formatted: Similarly, the simulated 95th and 99th percentiles were 11.070 and 15.072, respectively, compared with theoretical values of 11.071 and 15.086 (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S4</ref>).

text.text: Monte Carlo estimates of overall profile rarity also closely matched the corresponding theoretical tail probabilities.
For example, 4.9995% of simulated profiles exceeded the theoretical 5% threshold and 0.9949% exceeded the 1% threshold.
Differences between simulated and theoretical base rates were no greater than 0.032 percentage points across the criteria examined (Supplementary Table S5).
text.formatted: Differences between simulated and theoretical base rates were no greater than 0.032 percentage points across the criteria examined (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: These findings support the use of the theoretical χ²(5) distribution to estimate the normative rarity of WAIS-5 primary index profiles.

To further clarify the characteristics of cognitive profiles associated with MDI, its relationship with overall level and within-profile variability was examined across the simulated normative sample.
MDI was positively associated with both the absolute distance of the Mean Index Score from the normative mean of 100 (r s = .373) and the standard deviation of the five index scores (r s = .860).
Thus, although both characteristics were associated with MDI, the relationship was substantially stronger for within-profile variability than for overall level.
For clinical interpretation, MDI values corresponding to selected normative base rates are presented in Table 1.
text.formatted: For clinical interpretation, MDI values corresponding to selected normative base rates are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: An MDI of 11.07 or greater corresponds to an overall profile base rate of approximately 5% or less, while values of 13.39 and 15.09 correspond to base rates of approximately 2% and 1%, respectively.

Because calculation of the MDI requires matrix operations and is impractical to undertake manually in routine clinical practice, exact MDI values and corresponding base rates can be obtained using the accompanying calculator.
Note.
MDI values at or above each threshold indicate an overall profile base rate equal to or less than the corresponding percentage.
For example, an MDI of 11.07 or greater occurs in approximately 5% or less of the normative population.
MDI reflects the rarity of the overall configuration of primary index scores, taking into account their intercorrelations, and should not be interpreted as a measure of cognitive impairment.
Importantly, the MDI does not identify the features of the profile contributing to its rarity, which may reflect both the overall level and scatter of scores.
The following analyses therefore examine the occurrence of low scores, pairwise discrepancies, and deviations from the individual's mean level of performance.
The estimated base rates for obtaining multiple low primary index scores are presented in Table 2.
text.formatted: The estimated base rates for obtaining multiple low primary index scores are presented in Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: At the 25th percentile criterion, 59.57% of the normative population was estimated to obtain at least one low index score, compared with 42.08% at the 15th percentile, 31.02% at the 10th percentile, 17.60% at the 5th percentile, 7.87% at the 2nd percentile, and 4.14% at the 1st percentile.
Multiple low scores were progressively less common.
At the 15th percentile criterion, 19.62% of the normative population was estimated to obtain two or more low index scores and 9.03% three or more.
At the 5th percentile criterion, corresponding base rates were 5.20% for two or more low scores and 1.69% for three or more.
Obtaining four or five low index scores was uncommon at the more stringent criteria.
Full estimated base rates across all criteria are provided in Table 2.

Where multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies occur within an individual's profile, a further question is how unusual it is to observe that number of discrepancies together.
At the 15% criterion, 83.60% of the normative population exhibited at least one unusual pairwise discrepancy, 72.97% exhibited two or more, and 59.04% exhibited three or more (Table 3).

At the 2% criterion, 23.76% exhibited at least one unusual discrepancy, 10.70% exhibited two or more, and 4.05% exhibited three or more.

The rarity of each individual discrepancy was evaluated as a one-tailed probability, consistent with the WAIS-5 manual, rather than combining discrepancies in both directions as a two-tailed probability.
Discrepancies meeting the same rarity criterion were then counted together, regardless of which index was higher.
For example, four or more discrepancies each with a one-tailed base rate of 5% or less occurred in 7.09% of simulated normative profiles.

Appendix B of the WAIS-5 normative supplement (Wechsler et al., 2025b) provides critical values and empirical base rates for determining whether individual primary index scores represent relative strengths or weaknesses compared with the individual's own average (MIS).
text.formatted: Appendix B of the WAIS-5 normative supplement <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Wechsler et al., 2025b)</ref> provides critical values and empirical base rates for determining whether individual primary index scores represent relative strengths or weaknesses compared with the individual's own average (MIS).

text.text: These procedures evaluate individual strengths and weaknesses, but do not indicate how unusual it is to observe multiple relative strengths or weaknesses within the same cognitive profile.
The present analysis addressed this complementary question by estimating the normative base rates for obtaining increasing numbers of unusual strengths and weaknesses across the five primary indices.
To facilitate interpretation alongside the WAIS-5 strength/weakness procedure, the rarity of each individual strength or weakness was evaluated as a one-tailed probability.
At the 15% rarity criterion, 78.04% of simulated normative profiles exhibited one or more relative strengths or weaknesses, 50.57% exhibited two or more, and 16.57% exhibited three or more (Table 4).
text.formatted: At the 15% rarity criterion, 78.04% of simulated normative profiles exhibited one or more relative strengths or weaknesses, 50.57% exhibited two or more, and 16.57% exhibited three or more (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">4</ref>).

text.text: At the 5% criterion, corresponding base rates were 37.43%, 11.24%, and 1.21%, respectively.
At the 1% criterion, 9.07% exhibited one or more relative strengths or weaknesses, 0.92% exhibited two or more, and 0.03% exhibited three or more.
Cell values show how often the specified number of relative strengths and weaknesses occurred in the simulated normative population.
The rarity of each individual strength or weakness was evaluated as a one-tailed probability, consistent with the WAIS-5 manual.
Strengths and weaknesses meeting the same rarity criterion were then counted together.
For example, three or more strengths or weaknesses each with a one-tailed base rate of 5% or less occurred in 1.21% of simulated normative profiles.
In clinical practice, the meaning of an individual cognitive score depends partly on how it relates to the person's broader cognitive profile.

A low index score, a marked discrepancy, or a relative strength or weakness may appear noteworthy when considered alone, but its significance within a person's cognitive profile depends partly on how often such findings arise when the profile is considered as a whole.
This distinction matters because clinicians rarely encounter a single score in isolation.

A WAIS-5 assessment provides multiple, related opportunities to identify apparently unusual findings, and each additional comparison changes the context in which any one of those findings should be understood.
The multivariate approach developed by Crawford et al. (2012), and extended here to the WAIS-5, provides a way of placing those findings back into that broader context.
text.formatted: The multivariate approach developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref>, and extended here to the WAIS-5, provides a way of placing those findings back into that broader context.

text.text: The MDI addresses the person's profile at its broadest level by asking how unusual the overall configuration of their five index scores is.
Importantly, this is not the same as asking how unusual the person's overall level of cognitive performance is.
Although MDI was associated with both overall level and within-profile scatter, the association with scatter was substantially stronger (rₛ = .860 vs. rₛ = .373).
For example, a person with similarly low scores across all five indices may have a relatively common MDI despite a statistically rare (low or high) FSIQ.
Clinically, a common MDI should therefore not be taken to mean that the person's cognitive performance is unremarkable.
It means that the configuration of their index scores is not unusual.
When a person obtains a low index score, its percentile rank tells us how unusual that particular score is, but not how unusual it is to encounter a low score within their broader cognitive profile.
Low scores occur among healthy individuals, particularly when several measures are considered together (Binder et al., 2009; Kiselica et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Low scores occur among healthy individuals, particularly when several measures are considered together <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Binder et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kiselica et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Even across only five WAIS-5 indices, 17.60% of normative profiles contained at least one score at or below the 5th percentile, while 5.20% contained two or more.
While an index score at the 5th percentile is itself unusual, encountering at least one such score within a five-index profile is considerably less so.
The multivariate base rate provides this broader context by indicating how often the observed number of low scores would be expected within normative profiles.
Pairwise discrepancies present a particular challenge because five WAIS-5 indices generate ten possible comparisons.
At the directional 5% criterion, 46.47% of normative profiles contained at least one unusual discrepancy and 28.92% contained two or more.
A clinician may therefore commonly encounter several apparently unusual differences within a person's profile.

These findings are not independent: each index contributes to four pairwise comparisons, meaning that one relatively high or low score can produce several unusual discrepancies within the same person's profile.
Finding several uncommon discrepancies should not be interpreted as several independent pieces of evidence about that person's cognitive functioning (Crawford et al., 2007 (Crawford et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: Finding several uncommon discrepancies should not be interpreted as several independent pieces of evidence about that person's cognitive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: The profile-level base rate provides the necessary context by showing how unusual that collection of discrepancies is when the complete set of comparisons is considered.
Finally, relative strengths and weaknesses consider whether an index is unusual for the person given their own overall level of performance.
A score may be unremarkable when compared with population norms but stand out when considered alongside the person's other index scores, or vice versa (Crawford et al., 2012).
text.formatted: A score may be unremarkable when compared with population norms but stand out when considered alongside the person's other index scores, or vice versa <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying such a difference, however, does not necessarily mean that the pattern itself is unusual.
At the directional 5% criterion, at least one relative strength or weakness occurred in 37.43% of normative profiles, while two or more occurred in 11.24%.

For the clinician, the multivariate base rate helps distinguish between something that stands out within the person's profile and a pattern of strengths and weaknesses that is itself unusual in the normative population.
The practical value of these analyses lies in using them together without collapsing them into a single judgement.

Each provides a different perspective on the person's cognitive profile: whether the overall configuration of scores is unusual, whether the number of low scores is unusual, whether the observed discrepancies remain unusual when all possible comparisons are considered, and whether strengths and weaknesses within the person's own profile are themselves unusual.

Taken together, they provide a way of moving between the individual score, the relationships among scores, and the profile as a whole, while keeping clear what each analysis can and cannot tell us about the person's cognition.

The accompanying calculator is intended to make this process more feasible in routine clinical practice, providing the relevant base rates without requiring clinicians to undertake the underlying multivariate calculations.
The large number of simulated profiles that we were able to generate represents a particular strength of the present study.
Whereas Crawford et al. (2012) were able to generate 100,000 simulated WAIS-IV profiles, modern computational power allowed us to increase this to 1,000,000 simulated WAIS-5 profiles.
text.formatted: Whereas <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al. (2012)</ref> were able to generate 100,000 simulated WAIS-IV profiles, modern computational power allowed us to increase this to 1,000,000 simulated WAIS-5 profiles.

text.text: Perhaps because of that, our validation analyses showed that the simulated profiles closely reproduced the published WAIS-5 characteristics on which they were based, while the MDI distribution closely matched its theoretical expectations.
Importantly, these analyses do not represent new statistical methods but rather extend Crawford et al.'s established multivariate approach to accommodate the fiveindex structure of the WAIS-5.
These strengths should also be considered alongside several limitations.
The multivariate base rates were modelled from published WAIS-5 means, standard deviations, and intercorrelations rather than individual-level standardisation data.
Previous comparisons with empirical data have generally supported this approach, although small differences between simulated and observed base rates have been reported (Decker et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Previous comparisons with empirical data have generally supported this approach, although small differences between simulated and observed base rates have been reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Decker et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, previous studies suggest that simulated base rates tend to underestimate the occurrence of low scores among people with lower ability and overestimate their occurrence among those with higher ability (Brooks & Iverson, 2010).
text.formatted: Notably, previous studies suggest that simulated base rates tend to underestimate the occurrence of low scores among people with lower ability and overestimate their occurrence among those with higher ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Brooks & Iverson, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The present analyses were also conducted using the WAIS-5 Australian and New Zealand standardisation sample.
Since base rate estimates depend on the relationships among the five primary indices, differences in these relationships across standardisation samples may produce different multivariate base rates.

Replication using other WAIS-5 standardisations would help establish how well the present findings generalise and, where necessary, provide base-rate estimates appropriate to those normative populations.
A particularly important distinction for clinicians to bear in mind is the difference between statistical rarity and clinical significance.
The present analyses can tell us how unusual a person's WAIS-5 scores are, or wider cognitive profile is, within the normative population, but they cannot tell us why they are unusual.
A statistically rare profile may arise for many reasons and does not, by itself, establish a diagnosis, the presence of cognitive impairment or acquired change.
Equally, a statistically common profile does not exclude clinically important cognitive difficulties or meaningful change from the person's previous level of functioning.

Multivariate base rates should therefore inform, rather than determine, clinical interpretation (Crawford et al., 2012), alongside the person's history, circumstances, and broader assessment findings.
text.formatted: Multivariate base rates should therefore inform, rather than determine, clinical interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crawford et al., 2012)</ref>, alongside the person's history, circumstances, and broader assessment findings.

text.text: The present study extends Crawford et al.'s (2012) multivariate approach to the five primary indices of the WAIS-5 ANZ, providing normative base rates for the overall configuration of index scores, multiple low scores, pairwise discrepancies, and relative strengths and weaknesses.
text.formatted: The present study extends <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Crawford et al.'s (2012)</ref> multivariate approach to the five primary indices of the WAIS-5 ANZ, providing normative base rates for the overall configuration of index scores, multiple low scores, pairwise discrepancies, and relative strengths and weaknesses.

text.text: These analyses provide clinicians with a broader context for interpreting apparently unusual findings within an individual's cognitive profile.
Together with the accompanying calculator, they provide a practical framework for incorporating multivariate base rates into routine WAIS-5 interpretation.
